text.content:
Goal: a rigger (or anyone) designs their own vehicle by Rigger 2's rules (pp.108–146) and gets it on their character.

GM, once: turn on the Rigger 2 module (it brings the design tables and the modifications). To let players build their own, give them Create New Actors in Settings → Configure Permissions.

The designer

  1. Open the Workshop. On your character's Vehicles tab click Design a vehicle (the new vehicle is linked to you), or use Vehicle Workshop at the top of the Actors sidebar.
  2. Chassis. Pick a category (bikes, cars, boats, aircraft, drones…), then a chassis. Each card shows its Handling, Body, Cargo and Design Points.
  3. Power plant. Only the engines the book lists for that chassis are offered, grouped by fuel.
  4. Design options. Buy Speed, Acceleration, Load, Cargo, better Handling, Economy, fuel, Signature, smart materials, amenities, engine customization and so on. max buys up to the plant's maximum. A + that's greyed out has hit a limit (hover the row for the rule).
  5. Modifications. Search the catalog and click + to add. A row you can't add says why (wrong vehicle, needs another mod first…). Set ratings in the Installed table. Mods that change stats (turbocharging, drive-by-wire, suspension, armor…) show in the summary. Drive-by-wire asks how to split its one-time +10%.
  6. Price. Set the Mark-Up (luxury, security, military, unusual features). The price is Design Points × Mark-Up × 100¥.
  7. Review, name it at the top, and click Create vehicle.

Good to know

  • Anything wrong with the design (over the Load, over a maximum, a mod that doesn't fit) is listed in red in the summary, and the vehicle can't be saved until it's fixed.
  • To change a design later, open the vehicle's Design tab → Open the Workshop. Mods added on the sheet after the vehicle was built are customizations: they take space but cost no Design Points, and the Workshop leaves them alone.
  • Redesigning a vehicle that wasn't built in the Workshop (one from a compendium) asks first and shows what changes.

Goal: the decker walks up to a terminal on the map, jacks in, and only their screen moves to a Matrix map. Everyone else stays in meat space.

GM, once per location

  1. Make the Matrix scene. A new scene with the host's map (any image works; a dark scene with a coloured grid is fine). Give the players Limited or Observer permission on it, or their view can't follow. Draw a Region where personas arrive (the "entry area"). No behaviour is needed on it. Make it big enough for the whole team: each persona goes on its own free square inside it.

  2. Mark the jackpoint. On the real scene, draw a Region over the terminal or data port, where the decker will stand. In its config, Behaviors → + and pick Matrix jackpoint, then fill in:

    • Entry area on the Matrix scene: drag the entry Region from step 1 onto the field (or paste its UUID).
    • What it is (optional): the text on the Jack in button, e.g. "Strice mainframe port".
    • Host (optional): the Host actor the decker is most likely working against.
    • Trace modifier (VR2.0) (optional): added to the decker's Trace Factor here (Virtual Realities 2.0 p.28).

    When you save, the system warns you if the entry area is missing or no player can see the Matrix scene.

  3. Personas: nothing to do. When a decker jacks in, their persona token appears in the entry area (your client makes it, so you need to be logged in — if you weren't, it appears the moment you are). When they jack out it's removed.

    • Want a permanent one instead? Drag the decker onto the Matrix scene, right-click the token and click the astronaut button (Matrix persona). A hand-placed persona is used instead of a new one and stays between runs, dimmed while nobody is jacked in.
    • Like the one that appeared? Right-click it and click the pin button (Keep this persona): it becomes hand-placed and stays.
    • Anything on the entry area that reacts to a token entering (a Pause Game, a Teleport, a script) runs when a persona appears there, so you can use it as an alert.

At the table

  1. The decker moves their token into the jackpoint Region.

  2. They right-click their token: the HUD now has a network-port button, Jack in: (what it is). If it's greyed out, hover it for the reason (no working cyberdeck, not standing in the Region, …).

  3. They click it. Matrix mode goes on, a chat line says where they jacked in, their persona appears in the entry area, and only that player's screen switches to the Matrix scene, centred on it.

  4. Their body stays on the map with a cyan outline, so everyone can see who is jacked in (and vulnerable).

  5. To come back: Jack out (the plug with an ✕, where the Jack in button was) on the persona or the body. Dump shock, or the GM turning off Matrix mode on the sheet, also brings them back.

Tips

  • Player characters with linked tokens only. For an NPC decker, use the Matrix mode toggle on its sheet.

  • The sheet's own Jack In button never moves anyone's view: it's for tables that don't use Matrix maps.

  • A player can only follow one jacked-in character per browser window. A reload while jacked in puts them straight back on the Matrix scene.

  • The persona's look: the decker can pick a Matrix icon in the Persona box on their Matrix tab; blank uses their token image.

  • Deleting the jackpoint, its Region, the entry area or the Matrix scene ends any live session there. Pointing the jackpoint at a different entry area mid-run doesn't move a persona that's already in.

  • Deleting a persona that appeared on its own while the decker is in just brings a new one: jack them out to remove it.

  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: a corp facility has fat bacteria (FAB) in its walls and air. Astral intruders slow to a crawl inside, assensing from inside is harder, and with FAB-UV the guards can light it up and see a projecting mage (Corporate Security Handbook p.103).

GM, once per facility

  1. On the scene, draw a Region over the FAB-filled space (a room, a vault, the whole floor).
  2. In its config, Behaviors → + and pick Fat bacteria zone. Choose the Strain:
    • FAB-1: restricts astral movement only.
    • FAB-UV (glows under UV): also reveals astral intruders when the UV lights are on.
  3. Optional: set the Region's Visibility to Always if the players should see the zone drawn on the map (by default only the GM sees Regions, on the Regions layer).
  4. If the FAB is also in the walls, give those walls Astral barrier → Fat bacteria in their wall config: they then stop astral forms like a living wall (Astral Space).

What it does on its own

  • Movement: an astral form inside the zone is held to normal astral speed. Outside, a projecting magician can switch on fast astral movement from the form's token HUD (the ⏩ button): Magic in kilometres per action, but they can't assense or see detail. The speed caps are enforced in combat when Limit movement in combat is on (Game Settings).
  • Assensing: the eye button on an astrally active token's HUD rolls Assense (Sorcery or Conjuring, p.146). From inside the zone it takes +4 to the TN, shown on the roll.
  • Spellcasting and astral combat are not affected (the book).

Lighting it up (FAB-UV only)

  1. When the guards hit the UV, open the behaviour (Region config → the behaviour's gear) and tick UV lights on. Save.
  2. Select the guards doing the search (mundane tokens with an actor). Then click Search for astral intruders (selected tokens search) at the bottom of the behaviour's config.
  3. In the dialog, pick who rolls (the others lower the TN) and tick any intruder that knows it's being searched for: an aware intruder rolls Stealth against it.
  4. The roll: Perception (Intelligence), TN 6, +1 per 50 m² of zone, −1 per two searchers. The result goes to the GM in chat. Each intruder spotted becomes visible to everyone while it stays in the lit zone. Attacks against it are at +4, −1 per success beyond the first.

Tips

  • The reveal ends as soon as the intruder leaves the zone, the UV goes off, or the behaviour is disabled. Coming back in, or relighting, needs a new search.
  • Astral tokens of friendly disposition, and ones a player owns, are always visible to that player. Give an intruder hostile or neutral disposition, or the players will see it before anyone searches.
  • An unlinked NPC mage on the astral plane: mark its token astral-only from the token HUD (the crossed-out eye button) so mundane viewers can't see it.

Goal: a magician (and anyone who knows the same spell) casts a non-combat spell by ritual sorcery (p.133–137). The GM runs it; players roll when asked.

  1. Open the worksheet. On the leader's Magic tab, the GM clicks the ritual button (the circle of nodes) on the spell's row. Combat spells don't have one.
  2. Fill it in.
    • Force and the leader's Magic Pool dice.
    • Members: every other character who knows the spell is listed. Tick the ones taking part and set their pool dice. Pick an astral guide if one is used.
    • Subject: a targeted character, a specific place or object, or (area spells) an area you click on the map. Name it.
    • Tick Target in sight or astrally observed if no material link is needed (p.136), and the lodge / circle box if one rated at least the Force is ready.
    • The materials cost is shown: it's spent whatever happens.
  3. Start. The system checks the book's requirements and whispers the GM a ritual card. Everything from here is on that card, so the ritual can always be resumed from chat.
  4. Pay for materials. Charge materials takes the nuyen from the leader; Materials supplied if they're already on hand.
  5. Material link (skipped if the target is in sight). The test is rolled; players may spend Karma on it. Then Finalise link.
  6. Sending. Roll, then Finalise sending. Each stage records the time it took. The GM advances world time.
  7. Determine the effect. Choose how many Ritual Magic Pool dice to use and the TN, roll, then Finalise effect. Publish the effect posts the result (resist cards, healing, an area).
  8. Sustaining (sustained spells): Sustaining asks how. Not at all, with leftover pool dice (dice × the leader's Magic in hours), by an elemental (Force days), or with the team locked in (+2 to every member's Drain test).
  9. Drain. Every member gets a Resist Drain button on the card. Each rolls, then Finalise applies their damage.

If something goes wrong: Withdraw a member, Guide driven off and Terminate are on the card during the link, sending and effect stages. A stage with no successes aborts the ritual, and everyone still resists Drain (p.135).

Goal: a hermetic mage summons an elemental (p.140–142) and uses its services.

  1. Summon. On the Magic tab, click Summon Elemental. Pick the element and the Force. The rite's materials cost 1,000¥ × Force and are used up whether or not it works (untick Pay materials if the GM supplies them). Roll Conjuring, then resist the Charisma-based Drain.
    • Players need the GM to give them Create New Actors (Game Settings → Configure Permissions), or the summon stops before anything is rolled.
  2. It arrives away. The bound elemental is listed under Spirits with its services, but it has no token yet.
  3. Call it. Open the elemental's sheet and click Call. It appears on the map and its 24-hour clock starts.
  4. Use it.
    • Fight for me: one service for the whole fight. Stand down when it's over.
    • Aid Sorcery: when casting a spell of its element's category, the cast dialog has an Aid Sorcery section. Choose the elemental and how many of its dice go to the spell test and to Drain. Each die lowers its Force; starting the aid costs a service.
    • Aid Study: the Learn a spell dialog offers its Force in dice, once per spell (1 service).
    • Sustain a spell: on a sustained spell's row, click the hand icon. The elemental holds it (1 service), you lose the +2 TN, and it burns one point of Force per Combat Turn. Take the spell back (same icon) before its Force runs out, or the spell ends.
  5. Days. Each full day it's present costs a service: Charge day(s) when the sheet says it's owed.
  6. Send away returns it to astral space, on call. Re-call (1 service) brings it back at full Force. When the last service is spent, it departs.

See Spirits and Conjuring for nature spirits and banishing.

Goal: the Shadowtech drug rules (p.85–88) run themselves on game time. Needs the Shadowtech module.

  1. Take a dose. On the Gear tab, the syringe on the drug's row uses one dose: it rolls the duration and applies the effects. Active drugs shows the time left.
  2. Addiction and Tolerance tests. When the effect ends, a card offers the tests. The player rolls them from the card.
  3. Watch the Substances section. It lists each drug: doses taken, current Addiction and Tolerance (the printed values in brackets), whether the character is addicted (Physical, Mental or both), and when the next dose is due.
  4. Advance time. The section follows the GM's world clock. Advancing time in Foundry (or with Calendaria) makes doses come due, withdrawal start, and boxes or Essence go. "Substance time waits for a GM to connect" means no GM is online.
  5. Hold out longer (player, the hourglass): Body (physical) or Willpower (mental) against Addiction, once per dose.
  6. Recovery (GM): the walking figure starts recovery, Willpower vs Addiction +1 (mental), +3 (physical) or +4 (both). One substance at a time. Cleansing therapy (the hand) clears physical addiction and returns lost boxes. Gene cleansing (DNA icon) clears immunity.
  7. Corrections. The pencil records a hand correction. Nothing is deleted.

A character who was already a user: the GM gives them the drug item, then clicks Import history in the Substances header. Enter the doses taken so far, any boxes or Essence already lost, the hours since the last dose, and whether they're addicted now. Leave Addiction and Tolerance blank to have them worked out from the doses.

More in Gear, Buying and Drugs.

Goal: a decker writes their own utility, with options, and logs the days of work until it's done (Virtual Realities 2.0 pp.100–104).

GM, once: in Settings → Configure Settings → SR2E, set Matrix ruleset to Virtual Realities 2.0. For the options, also tick VR2.0 utility options. Everyone's client reloads.

The decker

  1. Start a project. On the Matrix tab, click the code button on the Programs header (Write a new program). A "New program" opens; it shows as unwritten until it's done.
  2. Design it. Name it after the utility (Attack, Browse, Armor…), set its Rating, and for an attack its Damage Level. With utility options on, + Add option adds options. One the utility can't take is struck through with the reason. The sheet shows the size and design size, and the price.
  3. Roll the test. Click the code button on the program's row. Tick any team members, then Roll: Computer against the program's rating. The card shows the base time ÷ your successes. You can still spend Karma on it.
  4. Log the work. Click the code button again for each stretch of work: days worked, and your tools (or each team member's bonus). The first log locks the test's successes. The row shows writing 4/10d.
  5. Done. When the days reach the period, the program is written and works like any other.

Good to know

  • The design is locked while it's being written. The ⊘ button abandons the work.
  • A program that fails its test (no successes) or is abandoned stays unwritten. Roll again to retry.
  • Black Hammer and Killjoy can't be written above half your Computer (rounded up). A team writes one point higher than its best member, with at most half that member's Computer in members.

Goal: a decker raises a program's rating, or adds options to it, without losing the version they have (Virtual Realities 2.0 p.107).

Needs: the Matrix ruleset on Virtual Realities 2.0 (GM settings); for options, VR2.0 utility options too. The program must have its source code: not ticked Object code only, or written by the decker.

The decker

  1. Upgrade. Click the ↑ button on the program's row. Set the new rating and tick any options to add (rated ones take a rating; Limit takes its target), then Next.
  2. Roll the test. Tick any team members, then Roll: Computer against the new rating. The base time is the new version's less the current one's, ÷ your successes.
  3. Log the work with the code button, as for writing. The row shows upgrading to 4 3/5d. The program still works at its old rating meanwhile, and its design is locked.
  4. Done. When the days reach the period, the new version replaces the old one (the GM's client writes it). If the row says upgrade done: applying for long, click ↑ again to resend it.

Good to know

  • No money moves: you programmed it. A loaded program counts as new object code.
  • Adding Limit makes the design smaller, so there's no base time: it's done on the test.
  • Command sets and frame cores can't be upgraded. The ⊘ button abandons an upgrade; the old version stays.

pages.name: Hit several IC with an Area attack (VR2.0)

text.content:
Goal: one Attack Test that hits more than one icon (Virtual Realities 2.0 p.103).

Needs: the Matrix ruleset on Virtual Realities 2.0 and VR2.0 utility options ticked (GM settings), and an attack utility with the Area option. Its rating is how many icons it can hit; give it a rating on the program's sheet. Write it yourself (Write a program) or add the option to one you have.

The decker

  1. Target the icons. Target the main one, then shift-click the others (up to the Area rating in all).
  2. Attack. Click Matrix Attack, pick the host and the Area program. The dialog lists your other targets under Area — also attack: tick the ones to include.
  3. One roll, a card per target. The dice are rolled once. Each target gets its own card, with its own target number (+1 for every target engaged) and its own successes.

The GM 4. Resist each card. Each target resists on its own card. IC armor (or a decker's Armor utility) gets +2 against an Area attack.

Good to know

  • Karma Pool on that shared roll is the GM's call, as for area spells.
  • Shield, Targeting, Penetration and the other options still apply per target.

pages.name: Draw IC off with a Decoy (VR2.0)

text.content:
Goal: a decker puts up a decoy copy of their icon so proactive IC attack it instead of them (Virtual Realities 2.0 p.112).

The decker

  1. On the Matrix tab, click System Operation, pick the host and Decoy (Control, Mirrors), and click Run. You need Mirrors loaded.
  2. If the test succeeds, the card says how strong the decoy is: your successes.

The GM, when IC attack

  1. Attack the decker as usual (target their token, then Matrix Attack on the IC). With a decoy up, the attack must come from the active GM's client.
  2. The system rolls 1D6 first. At or below the decoy's successes, the card says the decoy drew it.
  3. Click Hit the decoy: the damage goes on the decoy, not the decker. At 10 boxes the decoy is gone.

Tips

  • Trace IC ignores decoys.
  • One decoy at a time: a new successful Decoy replaces it. A failed one leaves the old decoy up.
  • The decoy lasts until it's destroyed, the decker logs on to another host, or jacks out.
  • A Karma reroll on the Decoy test changes the decoy's strength too.
  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: give the Matrix its shape, so deckers move from jackpoint to grid to host as the book describes (Virtual Realities 2.0 pp.14–30).

The GM, once

  1. Settings → Configure Settings → VR2.0 grid topology: tick it.
  2. In the Actors directory, click New grid and pick the RTG (or a German LTG) from the book's table. For a local grid of your own, open the RTG and click Create LTG.
  3. Open each host. In its Grid section, set Attached to its LTG. For a host reached only through another (a tiered network), leave that empty and Link it to the host in front of it.
  4. For a corporate PLTG, set the host's Kind to PLTG and add its Entry points (LTGs).
  5. Tick Unlisted address on anything the deckers must find first.
  6. On each jackpoint behaviour, set its kind. Set Wired to to its LTG (a trid jackpoint) or to the host it controls (a workstation, remote device or console).

The decker

  1. Jack in. The Matrix tab says At the jackpoint.
  2. System Operation: the dialog offers only what you can reach. Log on to the LTG, then to a host on it.
  3. To move to another host on the same grid, log on to it directly. To go back up, click Disconnect to grid.

Tips

  • An RTG and its LTGs share one security tally, so the RTG's sheaf is the one to fill in.
  • A PLTG inherits the public tally when you get in, and its triggers can go off at once.
  • Can't find a host? Run Locate Access Node on the RTG. On a success, the GM reveals its address.
  • Jacking out at the jackpoint, before logging on to anything, is free.
  • Each host's sheet lists what's Reachable from here.
  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: reach a host that sits behind a corporate hub, and shake the hub's trace IC on the way (Virtual Realities 2.0 p.36). Needs VR2.0 grid topology on.

The GM, once

  1. Attach the hub to its LTG (Attached to in its Grid section).
  2. On each host behind it, leave Attached to empty and Link it to the hub.
  3. Optional: on the hub, set Connections hidden in to a subsystem other than Access.

The decker

  1. Log on to the hub.
  2. System Operation → Analyze Subsystem on the hub, with the targeted subsystem set to Access (or wherever the GM hid the connections). On a success, a card says you've found them.
  3. System Operation → Logon to Host and pick the host behind the hub. If the hub's trace IC is hunting you, its rating is added to the TN: leaving counts as a Graceful Logoff.
  4. On a success the hub loses your datatrail: its trace crashes, and the hub forgets your tally.

Tips

  • To reach another host behind the hub, log on back to the hub first, then onward. Hosts behind it aren't linked to each other.
  • Locate File or Locate Slave on the hub searches the whole network.
  • On a public grid, a trace IC loses interest as soon as you log on to a host.
  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: jack in through a communications satellite, so a trace can find the satellite but never the decker (Virtual Realities 2.0 p.30). Needs VR2.0 grid topology on.

The GM, once

  1. In the Actors directory, New grid → Create satellite. Pick Orange-Average for a communications satellite, or Red-Hard for a military or corporate one.
  2. Draw a Region where the dish is and give it the Matrix jackpoint behaviour. Set Kind to Satellite uplink, and Wired to to the satellite (or leave it empty for any satellite).

The decker

  1. On the deck (or the Matrix tab's cyberdeck block), tick Satlink and pick your dish.
  2. Jack in at the uplink. The Matrix tab shows Locate satellite: pick the satellite and the conditions (downtown is hardest; a large dish or a fixed-base station helps). Bad weather adds 2.
  3. On a success you lock onto it. On a miss, try again in about five minutes; Karma can buy the success.
  4. System Operation → Logon to LTG onto the satellite, then Logon to RTG to any RTG on earth.

Tips

  • The uplink is +2 to every Access Test, and signal lag costs −2 Reaction.
  • The satellite's security tally follows you into the RTG you log on to.
  • A trace that completes finds only the satellite: no physical response, and the grid can't dump you.
  • More in The Matrix.

pages.name: Build and load a frame core (VR2.0)

text.content:
Goal: write a frame core and load programs onto it (Virtual Realities 2.0 pp.105–106). Running frames on a host comes in a later release.

Write the core

  1. On the Matrix tab, add a new program and open it. Set Frame core to Dumb or Smart and its rating (the Core Rating).
  2. Give it Bod, Evasion, Masking and Sensor: together no more than the Core Rating. A smart core needs a DINAB option (no higher than your Computer) and can put points into Initiative.
  3. Click the programming button (</>) on its row and write it as any program.

Load it

  1. Click Load programs… (the box icon) on the core's row and tick the programs: their ratings may total the Core Rating less its Initiative points.
  2. Roll the loading test, then log days with the same button until it's done.
  3. The row lists the loaded copies and the frame's size.

Tips

  • The copies are frozen: improving a program later doesn't change a loaded frame. Load again to take the new version.
  • Changing the core's attributes means writing a new core, and its old load no longer counts.
  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: put a frame you've built onto a host, where it runs as its own icon (Virtual Realities 2.0 pp.105–107). The server must have been restarted since the update to 0.136.0 (a new actor type).

The decker

  1. Build and load a frame core (see Build and load a frame core).
  2. Jack in and log on to the host where it should run.
  3. Click the upload icon on the core's row. If the core is squeezed, click Decompress frame first.
  4. Stay on the host until the upload finishes. The chat card says how long it takes.

The GM

  • In combat, the upload counts down by itself, 3 seconds per round.
  • Outside combat, click Upload finished (GM) on the card when that time has passed.
  • The frame appears as a Frame actor, and as a token beside the decker's persona if it has one on a Matrix scene.

Tips

  • A dumb frame crashes as soon as its decker leaves that host. A smart one keeps running.
  • Frames can be attacked: they resist with their own Bod and their Armor copy, and crash at 10 boxes.
  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: make a running dumb frame work for you: run an operation, attack, or act as a decoy (Virtual Realities 2.0 pp.106–107).

The decker

  1. Upload a dumb frame and stay on its host (see Upload and run a frame).
  2. On the Matrix tab, click Command… on the frame's row.
  3. Pick what it does: a System Operation, an attack or Scan Icon or a maneuver (target the icon first), or an event trigger. Set your Hacking Pool and Karma as for your own tests.
  4. Each command is a Simple Action of yours. For another attack, give another command.

A decoy frame

  1. Command the frame to run Decoy (it needs a Mirrors program).
  2. While you stay inactive, every IC attack on you goes to the frame instead. A Null Operation still counts as waiting.
  3. Your own next action ends it: chat says so.

The GM

  • Roll IC attacks on a decker with a decoy frame yourself: the system sends them to the frame.
  • Fire an event trigger from the frame's sheet when the event happens.

Tips

  • A core with DINAB can run a program for free once per action: tick Run by the core's DINAB.
  • Cripplers lower a frame's attributes; its sheet shows "Bod 1 of 3" and so on.
  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: put a smart frame to work: it acts on its own turns, with its own skill and tally (Virtual Realities 2.0 pp.105–107).

The decker

  1. Build, load and upload a smart frame core (see Build and load a frame core and Upload and run a frame).
  2. On its host, click Order… on the frame's row and type its basic order. It's a Free Action.

Running the frame (the decker's player, or the GM)

  1. Open the frame's sheet and click Act….
  2. Pick a System Operation, or target an icon and pick an attack, Scan Icon or a maneuver.
  3. The frame rolls its DINAB rating; its own tally rises on its sheet.

In combat

  • The frame joins a combat its decker fights in, with Core Rating + 1D6 (+1 die per Initiative point), and acts on its own turns. Remove it from the tracker and it stays out.

Tips

  • It keeps running after the decker jacks out, until it crashes or its host shuts down.
  • Trace IC can't trace a smart frame. Decoy needs a dumb frame.
  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: put a semi-autonomous knowbot into a run: create it, give it utilities, and move it between hosts (Virtual Realities 2.0 pp.140–141). This is the GM's.

Create it

  1. Make its native host (a Host actor).
  2. In the Actor Directory, click New SK. Pick the native host and a preset, or leave MPCP and the pool blank to roll them.

Give it utilities

  1. On its sheet, click Allocate…. Type a utility and its rating on each row (up to its MPCP), and pick Initiative points.
  2. Black hammer and killjoy cost 2 points per rating point. Restore and medic points stay until it has been home.

Run it

  • Act…: an operation, an attack, Scan Icon or a maneuver, with its MPCP as its skill.
  • Graceful Logoff to leave a host, then Logon to Host… to arrive elsewhere. Home needs no test.
  • Damaged? Log it on to its native host: it's repaired. Already home: Regenerate.

Tips

  • Add it to a combat from its token, like IC.
  • Ten boxes crash it for good; the sheet stays as a record.
  • More in The Matrix.

Goal: leave orders on a host that run later, like opening a security door at a set time (Virtual Realities 2.0 pp.104–105).

The decker

  1. Log on to the host. On the Matrix tab, click Command set….
  2. Name it, write the orders, and pick its tests (the GM says which: Slave for a device, Files for a file, Access for a SAN, Control when in doubt).
  3. Click Test beside the set on the Matrix tab, roll, spend any Karma, then Settle step on the card. Repeat for each test.

A complex set

  1. New command-set program (Matrix tab) creates the program: its size rolls 1D6 × 20 Mp.
  2. In Command set…, pick it: it uploads like a frame. When the upload finishes, a Control Test loads it, then its tests.

The GM

  • The host's sheet lists each set: its tests, its status, and how long it stays undetected (24 ÷ the host's successes, in hours; 48 if none).
  • Mark it Executed when it runs its orders, Purged if security finds it early, or Cancel an unfinished one.

Tips
